title: Possibility of Mets trading Francisco Lindor remains unlikely: Sources
content:
While the possibility exists that the New York Mets end up trading Francisco Lindor, multiple executives across the industry described the chances on Friday as unlikely.

The Mets are open to listening to offers for nearly all of their players. Lindor is not among the exceptions. Any team that expresses interest in the star shortstop, however, would have to clear a high bar.

The Mets viewing Lindor as a valuable player is just one reason people with knowledge of the situation, who were granted anonymity for their candor, don’t see a trade happening. There are a handful of other reasons, too. Chief among them is that Lindor, 32, owns trade veto power and is owed more than $160 million after this season through 2031.

New York does not hold a particular interest in paying down Lindor’s contract in a potential trade because, in its view, he can still be part of a winning team next year. A potential lockout is threatening the 2027 season, but the Mets, who are all but certain to miss the postseason for a second consecutive year, want to win whenever there is a next season.

Lindor declined to comment when The Athletic brought up his no-trade power during a recent conversation. As a 10-year veteran who has played the past five consecutive years with the same team, Lindor holds veto power over any potential trade.

Lindor actively engages in any conversation concerning the Mets’ future. A person close to him said he doesn’t want out of New York; he is comfortable with the team and loves the city — and wants to win with the Mets.

The Mets (41-57) are fielding calls as sellers in a market lacking them. They are not expected to engage in any trade talks regarding Juan Soto, Nolan McLean, Christian Scott, A.J. Ewing or Carson Benge, as SNY first reported Thursday.

Lindor is different, and his talent stands out in a cloudy trade market full of teams still competing for the playoffs. Still, he is in the middle of a challenging individual season. Defensively, he has made a few mental lapses in addition to errors on routine plays. He is typically as sure-handed as it gets, but defensive metrics this season rank him as mediocre. Offensively, Lindor is hitting just .210 with a .654 OPS.

Injuries have limited Lindor, generally a slow starter, to just 41 games and 175 plate appearances. No doubt, the missed time has played a role in his poor numbers. Hamate bone surgery robbed Lindor of a normal spring training. He was just getting hot at the plate when a calf injury sidelined him for two months. After a short rehab assignment, he returned from the injured list on June 24.

Lindor may be showing signs of some decline, but it’s also probably unwise to count him out completely. He is just one season removed from performing as a steady MVP-caliber player. In each of the past four seasons, Lindor finished within the top 10 in balloting for the NL MVP Award.

Mets starter Clay Holmes, out since mid-May because of a fibula fracture, is expected to make a rehab start Saturday with High-A Brooklyn, according to people with knowledge of the club’s plans who spoke on the condition of anonymity because things weren’t completely finalized.

Holmes is a significant trade candidate. He threw a live bullpen session Tuesday. Multiple teams are expected to scout his first rehab outing Saturday.

Holmes, 33, holds a player option worth $12 million for 2027 and is also a candidate for an extension. His 2026 season got off to a fantastic start. Over nine starts, he holds a 2.39 ERA.
